reviews.plausible_gain_reasoning: By the auditor's own energy balance the gel dissipates ~0.02% of near-wall turbulence production, so no measurable friction reduction; with U/c_s ~ 0.95 the risk of hydroelastic surface waves makes a drag increase as likely as a decrease.
key_assumption_issues: No drag quantity was simulated; the field only gives surface compliance, and no baseline was simulated.
Quasi-static loading by p'_rms ignores the frequency dependence of the gel modulus (G rises with frequency, reducing compliance at 300 Hz).
The sea-ice analogy concerns long ocean waves at Hz frequencies, not kHz-range near-wall turbulence.
killer_risks: Shear-wave speed ~7.4 m/s equals cruising speed: hydroelastic instability can roughen the surface and raise drag.
tan delta ~ 1 gels have very low tear and abrasion resistance; fender and cleaning damage within the first year.
3 mm silicone build is 5-8x the cost of standard foul release.

reviews.plausible_gain_reasoning: Flush tiles are at best hydraulically smooth, so friction equals the clean baseline; the 14.7% is a fouling-release stress reduction and it relies on a rigid-tile translation mode that barnacle bases spanning several tiles may not see.
key_assumption_issues: Metric is fouling detachment stress, not drag.
Compliance modelled as uniform foundation shear under a rigid tile; tile rocking/peel at gaps, which is the claimed advantage, is not modelled.
Adhesion work of 0.3 J/m2 on tiles vs 0.05 on silicone is an assumed, influential input (gain sign depends on it).
killer_risks: Water ingress and cracks start at the tile gaps; tiles debond after thermal cycling.
Hard tile surfaces foul more strongly than silicone at low speeds, and release is only marginally easier than standard foul release.
Laying millions of tiles or laminating mosaic films over curved hull areas is slow and expensive.
